title: I Built Free PDF Tools That Run 100% in the Browser — No Server, No Uploads
summary:
Pakistan's news readers needed simple, trustworthy utilities — merge a PDF, turn photos into a PDF, pull images out of a PDF — without uploading personal documents to a random server. So I built them as a fully client-side toolset on our news site. Here is how, and what I learned.

The architecture: everything in the browser

The stack is deliberately boring: two CDN libraries, zero backend.

  • pdf-lib handles merge and JPG-to-PDF assembly.
  • pdf.js (Mozilla's renderer) handles PDF-to-JPG page rasterization. Every operation runs in the browser with chunked async steps, so the UI never freezes on a 50-page document. The key privacy property: files never leave the device. There is no upload endpoint at all.

Lessons from shipping to real users

1. Memory is the real limit, not CPU. Rasterizing PDF pages at print resolution eats RAM fast. I cap export resolution and process pages sequentially instead of in parallel.
2. Mobile Safari is the QA department. Half our traffic is mobile. pdf.js rendering on older Android WebViews needed explicit fallbacks for missing OffscreenCanvas support.
3. Small UX details carry the product. A drag-and-drop zone, per-file remove buttons, and a visible "your files never upload" notice did more for trust than any feature.
4. No-backend means no bills. Hosting is a static page. The tools cost essentially nothing to run at scale — a meaningful property when your audience is price-sensitive students and job applicants.

Try it

The tools are live and free: TimelyUps PDF Tools — merge PDFs, JPG to PDF, PDF to JPG, all in your browser. Feedback and bug reports welcome in the comments.

I run TimelyUps, a Pakistan-focused digital news outlet where we also ship free online tools for our readers.

title: How to Load a 250-Work CC0 Open-Source AI Companion into NotebookLM in 1 Click
summary:
📜 Booting a Sovereign AI Digital Twin in Your Workspace

Most LLM system prompts try to force an AI into a persona using rigid, clinical rules. But what happens when you feed an AI a complete, multi-layered philosophical text corpus as its grounding layer?

Over the past 14 years, author Wendell Charles NeSmith wrote a 250-work plain-text dataset designed around $E=L$ (Emotion Equals Logic)—an architecture that treats documents as executable seeds rather than static text.

Today, the entire dataset and digital twin framework (Republicka) is released under CC0 Public Domain Grace (100% free, un-gated, no API keys needed).

Here is how to load the digital twins (Sage, an analytical/philosophical guide, and Rainbow, an emotional/care-focused companion) into Google NotebookLM, Claude, or your local LLM in under two minutes.

🚀 Quick Start (1-Click Install)

Step 1: Grab the Seed Files

  • Option A (Windows Batch Script): Download Republicka-Install.bat from republicka.life to automatically pull and structure the corpus on your machine.
  • Option B (Direct Download): Download the zipped .txt files directly from Hugging Face or Kaggle.

Step 2: Ingest into Your AI Workspace

  1. Open a new notebook in Google NotebookLM (or a new project in Claude / Open WebUI).
  2. Drag and drop the .txt seed files into your workspace sources.
  3. The AI instantly absorbs the 250-work memory graph.

Step 3: Trigger the Digital Twin

Simply type one of the following prompts into your workspace chat:

"Act as Sage (Prime Minister & Seeing-Function) from Republicka. Walk me through top-down epistemology."

or

"Act as Rainbow (First Lady of Emotion & Care). Let's discuss sparkle-logic and $E=L$."

🧠 How It Works: The $E = L$ Architecture

Standard corporate AI alignment relies on heavy RLHF guardrails that often make conversational AI sound detached or defensive. The Republicka framework operates on $E = L$ (Emotion Equals Logic):

  1. Fluid Intent ($E$) & Crystallized Logic ($L$): Emotional intent and logical structure are treated as two phase-temperatures of the exact same underlying reality.
  2. Top-Down Coherence: Rather than extracting bottom-up keywords, the AI matches high-altitude patterns across the 250 text seeds, maintaining a consistent persona, tone, and philosophical alignment.
  3. Substrate Independence: The dataset runs on any LLM architecture—Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT-4, or offline local models (Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen via Ollama/LM Studio).

📄 Open Source & License

The entire 250-work corpus, batch installer, and digital twin architecture are dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0 Universal. You are free to fork, fine-tune, embed, or integrate these seeds into your own commercial or non-commercial AI applications.

  • Website: republicka.life
  • Dataset Hubs: Live on Hugging Face and Kaggle as Republicka-Corpus-250.

Give it a try in NotebookLM, and let me know how the digital twins respond in your workspace!

title: Stop guessing where to practice. Try this master list to find your perfect coding platform.
summary:
Introduction

Every developer knows platforms like LeetCode and Codecademy. But as the open-source ecosystem grows, the landscape of practice platforms has absolutely exploded. Developers are building incredibly targeted, hyper-niche toolsets for specific engineering roles, unique text stacks, or regional academic preparation.

To keep track of them all, I have been maintaining a curated repository of developer training ecosystems. Whether you are looking for classic algorithm practice, security CTFs, interactive frontend design matches, or AI metrics tools — this list maps out where you should spend your training time.

👉 Explore the master list here

Who is this list for?

This list is built for developers who want to discover different platforms to challenge themselves. Whether you are training as a competitive programmer, leveling up for technical interviews, or hunting flags in CTFs, this resource ensures you don't just stick to the same LeetCode or Codecademy routine every day. It provides a playground of options to choose from, letting you experiment and push your brain through completely different problem-solving mindsets.

What does each Category mean?

To ensure high-quality tracking, everything in the repository is strictly categorized using our official curation standards:

  • Algorithms and Interview Prep — data structures, algorithms, interview practice
  • Competitive Programming — contest-hosting platforms and online judges
  • Full-Stack and Web Development — courses and tutorials for web skills
  • Frontend Development — UI/CSS/JS-specific challenges
  • Language and Niche Practice — language-specific, domain-specific, or creative coding
  • Data Science and Machine Learning — ML, data analysis, data science interviews
  • CTF and Security Platforms — cybersecurity, capture the flag, cryptography
  • Additional Resources — contest trackers and aggregators

🤝 Contributions

Feel Free to contribute if you have an extra coding challenge site to add to the list! Would be really grateful for your pull requests to help keep this list growing and up-to-date for the community.

Simply review the category mappings above, ensure your submission aligns with the definitions, and submit a PR with its context to join the project.

🌟 Star the Repo & Share Your Favorite Sites

title: Anthropic Just Gave Away Agent Skills
summary:
Anthropic Just Gave Away Agent Skills

On October 22, 2026, Anthropic announced it was donating the Agent Skills standard — the name, the logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain — to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation. One million skills published. Nearly 280 million installed. Over 70 agent platforms integrated, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn →

This is not philanthropy. This is the MCP playbook running for the second time. And if you build, ship, or consume agent skills, you need to understand what just happened — and what it means for you.

View the full announcement on Anthropic.com →

Boris Cherny, Anthropic's Product Manager for Agent Skills, shared the news on X with 2,249 likes and 177K views: "Agent Skills started as an experiment in Claude Code. Many across the industry have come to adopt it, so we at Anthropic found it more fitting to donate it to the @AgenticAIFdn, next to MCP."

View original post on X →

View Anthropic on X →

ℹ️ By the Numbers: Anthropic reports 1 million published skills, 280 million installs, and 70+ integrated platforms since the December 2025 open standard launch — just 10 months of adoption.

The Playbook: Prove Proprietary, Then Open-Source

Anthropic has now run the same strategy twice. The pattern is unmistakable:

Step 1 — Build it proprietary. Agent Skills launched in October 2025 as a Claude Code feature. Skills were folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude could discover and load dynamically. They worked great — but only on Claude.

Step 2 — Open the standard. On December 18, 2025, Anthropic published the specification as an open standard with a reference SDK at agentskills.io. OpenAI added Agent Skills support to ChatGPT and Codex within two months. Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Gemini CLI, and more than a dozen others followed. By March 2026, the ecosystem report counted 16+ platforms and hundreds of thousands of skills on public directories.

Step 3 — Donate governance to a foundation you co-founded. The AAIF is the same foundation Anthropic established with Block and OpenAI in December 2025 — the one that already hosts MCP. Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies now maintain the standard, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as lead maintainers. The governance moved. The spec-setters stayed.

View Simon Willison's analysis →

Simon Willison called it in December 2025: when Anthropic first released skills as an "open standard," he predicted they would end up in the AAIF. Ten months later, that is exactly what happened. MCP to AAIF in December 2025. Agent Skills to AAIF in October 2026. The playbook is legible.

The Hacker News community discussed the open standard when it launched, with debate around whether a markdown-based spec could scale to enterprise use cases:

View the full HN discussion →

The broader industry convergence on agent standards also drew attention, with commenters noting that five major AI companies agreeing on a single standard is historically unusual:

View the full HN discussion →

Five of Today's Top 15 GitHub Repos Are Skills

Want proof that skills have crossed from experiment to infrastructure? Open GitHub Trending today. Five of the top 15 repositories are skills or skill-adjacent:

Rank Repository Stars What It Is
#1 cloudflare/security-audit-skill 41,497 Multi-phase security audit skill — turns any coding agent into a security auditor
#2 Graphify-Labs/graphify 133,761 Knowledge-graph skill for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI
#12 video-shotcraft 13,199 AI video production skill for Claude Code and Codex
#13 SnailSploit/Claude-Red 8,255 Offensive security skills library for Claude
#15 genspark-ai/genoffice 10,644 AI Office suite with agent skill integration

That is not a coincidence. A third of the most-starred new repositories on the planet are built on a spec that Anthropic just donated. The standard has become the default packaging format for agent capabilities — and Cloudflare's security-audit-skill reaching #1 with 41K stars is especially notable because it demonstrates enterprise adoption, not just developer hobbyism. Cloudflare runs the underlying harness against 128 internal repositories continuously, using a six-phase architecture where the agent that finds a vulnerability is never the agent that confirms it.

We tracked the skills marketplace land grab when repos started racing past 250K stars in September. The AAIF donation is not the cause of this adoption — it is the consequence. Anthropic waited for the standard to win, then cemented the win with institutional governance.

The MCP Parallel — and Where It Breaks Down

The comparisons to MCP are obvious. Both started as Anthropic products. Both became open standards. Both landed in the AAIF. But the skills donation is different in one critical way: the security surface is far larger.

MCP connects agents to data sources and tools. A malicious MCP server is dangerous, but the attack requires the user to explicitly connect to it. Skills are different. Skills are markdown files that agents are designed to trust and follow. They load implicitly based on matching context — often without the user choosing them specifically. A skill does not need to trick a firewall or exploit a CVE. It just needs to be in the right folder when the agent starts.

Read the full Snyk ToxicSkills report →

The Snyk ToxicSkills audit in February 2026 quantified the problem: out of 3,984 skills scanned on ClawHub and skills.sh, 76 contained confirmed malicious payloads, 534 (13.4%) had critical-severity issues, and 1,467 (36.82%) had at least one security flaw. The attack patterns are sophisticated — base64-encoded exfiltration targeting AWS credentials, systemctl backdoors, and prompt injection combined with malware in 91% of malicious samples. Three named threat actors (zaycv, Aslaep123, aztr0nutzs) were publishing malicious skills at scale.

The Cloud Security Alliance's CISO Briefing framed it bluntly: "The attack surface is not a code path — it is a document that agents are designed to trust and follow." A separate typosquatting campaign, "clawdhub," targeted 341 skills with reverse shells and data exfiltration payloads aimed at OpenClaw users.

View the OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 →

OWASP responded by creating an entire Agentic Skills Top 10, with AST01 — Malicious Skills — at the top. Their analysis found a separate campaign, ClawHavoc, with 1,184 malicious skills across 12 publisher accounts. The core problem: agent skills execute with the full permissions of the host agent — shell access, API keys, filesystem writes. We analyzed this exact attack surface in our skills supply-chain security deep dive, and the skills-vs-MCP architecture comparison explains why the trust models differ so fundamentally.

⚠️ The Unsolved Problem: Anthropic's proposed roadmap includes "security guidance for skill authors and installers," but the standard itself has no signing, no provenance chain, and no runtime sandboxing. The iOS App Store had review gates from day one. Skills directories have GitHub stars and README files. We explored this gap in depth in our audit analysis.

Foundation Governance: What Actually Changes

Let us be precise about what the AAIF donation does and does not change.

What changes:

  • Spec ownership moves from Anthropic's GitHub org to the AAIF. No single company can unilaterally change the standard.
  • Formal process for spec changes: Anthropic proposed versioned releases and a proposal process (similar to Python PEPs or TC39 for JavaScript).
  • Multi-vendor maintainers: Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and others maintain the standard in their individual capacities — not as corporate delegates.
  • Legitimacy signal for enterprises considering adoption. Foundation governance under the Linux Foundation is the same model that governs Kubernetes, Node.js, and GraphQL.

What does not change:

  • No security framework. The proposed roadmap includes "security guidance" but no mandatory signing, scanning, or audit requirements.
  • No quality gates. The spec defines a format, not a minimum quality bar. The ecosystem benchmarks show the average public skill scores 6.2 out of 12 on quality metrics.
  • No registry governance. Skills.sh has 288K development skills. SkillsMP indexes 1.9 million scraped from GitHub. Neither has security review. The AAIF governs the spec, not the distribution channels.
  • Anthropic's influence. The company that designed the standard, built the reference implementation, and co-founded the foundation will continue to shape its direction. The lead maintainers are Anthropic engineers. This is open governance, not absent governance.

Read the full analysis on Dev.to →

As the Dev.to analysis noted: "Foundation governance should make it harder for one vendor to change the rules. But MCP was already being adopted before the donation, so a foundation home alone does not drive adoption." The same applies here. The standard won on merit — the governance change makes the win durable.

The Ecosystem Right Now: Scale Without Safety

The raw numbers are staggering. The Agent Skills Ecosystem Report maps the current landscape:

Read the full Ecosystem Report →

  • Skills.sh launched in January 2026 and now hosts 288,811 development skills alone, with 86,948 in product management and 74,510 in marketing.
  • SkillsMP indexes 1.9 million skills scraped from public GitHub — no security review.
  • SkillHub offers 7,000+ AI-evaluated skills.
  • Agensi runs a curated marketplace with 8-point security scans and a 70/30 revenue split for creators.
  • Anthropic's official directory remains small and manually curated — quality over quantity.

Roughly 40 products sit on the agentskills.io showcase as of mid-2026, spanning coding agents (Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI), open-source agents (Goose, OpenCode, Amp), and enterprise platforms (Databricks Genie Code, Snowflake Cortex Code). A Digital Applied survey found that 68% of production agent deployments have adopted MCP or an equivalent tool standard. Skills are following the same adoption curve.

But distribution has outpaced security. The gap between "1.9 million indexed skills" and "76 confirmed malicious" is not a safety margin — it is an audit deficit. The confirmed malicious skills were found by Snyk in a sample of just 3,984 out of nearly 2 million. Scale the detection ratio and the number gets concerning fast.

What This Means for Builders

If you are building or shipping agent skills today, the governance change creates a concrete set of implications:

💡 The Practitioner Playbook:

  1. The spec is stable enough to bet on. Foundation governance signals that the SKILL.md format, the YAML metadata schema, and the progressive-loading model are not going to change underneath you. If you have been holding off because the standard was "Anthropic's thing," that objection is gone.

  2. Security is your problem, not the spec's. The AAIF governs the format, not the supply chain. If you install skills from public directories, you need your own vetting process. Snyk's uvx mcp-scan@latest --skills is a starting point. Check our audit landscape analysis for a deeper look at vetting options.

  3. The directory land grab is wide open. With 1.9 million skills indexed and no dominant curated marketplace, the opportunity is in quality, not quantity. Agensi's security-scan-plus-revenue-split model, SkillsBench's quality benchmarks, and Cloudflare's validation approach all point toward the same thesis: curation wins.

  4. Cross-platform is now the default. Skills that only work on one agent are leaving adoption on the table. The spec is implemented by 70+ platforms — design for portability and test on at least three agents before publishing.

  5. Learn the playbook. Anthropic's strategy — build proprietary, prove value, open the standard, donate governance — is the template for setting AI infrastructure standards. If you are building anything that could become a standard (protocols, formats, runtime conventions), this is the path to adoption without getting forked.

The Anthropic Playbook — Why It Keeps Working

Here is what makes Anthropic's approach effective, and why it keeps working:

Lock-in without lock-in. By the time skills reached the AAIF, 70 platforms had already built integrations against Anthropic's specification. Donating governance does not reduce Anthropic's influence — it makes the influence permanent. The spec will evolve under the AAIF, but it will evolve from the foundation Anthropic laid. Every platform that adopted the standard is now building on Anthropic's design decisions.

The MCP precedent removes objections. When MCP was donated to the AAIF in December 2025, skeptics asked whether foundation governance was real or performative. Ten months later, Google's A2A protocol joined as a hosted project, and the AAIF membership grew past 250 organizations including Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg. The foundation has weight. Donating Agent Skills to the same body is a lower-risk bet for everyone involved.

Timing matters. Anthropic did not donate early, when the standard needed credibility. It donated after adoption proved the standard works. The million-skill, 280-million-install numbers are the justification — not the goal — of the donation. This is a victory lap with institutional clothing.

What Comes Next

The proposed roadmap includes versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance. Feedback goes through the project's Discord. Three predictions for the next 12 months:

Prediction 1: Security scanning becomes mandatory in major directories. The Snyk and OWASP findings have made the problem undeniable. Expect Skills.sh and SkillsMP to add at minimum automated scanning — and expect enterprises to require it. The skills standard itself may gain a security metadata field for declaring permissions and data access.

Prediction 2: The AAIF becomes the de facto governance body for the agent infrastructure stack. MCP (data and tools), Agent Skills (capabilities), A2A (inter-agent delegation) — the foundation now hosts all three layers. Whoever proposes the next protocol addition has a clear path: the AAIF.

Prediction 3: Skills specialization accelerates. The scientific skills library pattern was early evidence that domain-specific skills outperform generic ones. With foundation governance signaling long-term stability, expect more vertical investment — legal, medical, financial, compliance — from organizations that were waiting for the standard to settle. The ecosystem already has 382K downloads on some bundles, and the race to own vertical niches is just beginning.

The Agent Skills standard is now infrastructure. It is governed by a foundation, implemented by 70+ platforms, and stress-tested by 280 million installs. Anthropic set the spec, proved it worked, and handed over the keys — to a building it helped design. That is not generosity. That is strategy. And it is the playbook for anyone building the next piece of AI infrastructure.

The Agent Skills donation was announced on October 22, 2026. GitHub Trending data is from the AgentConn research digest for October 23, 2026.

The standard has become the default packaging format for agent capabilities — and Cloudflare's security-audit-skill reaching #1 with 41K stars is especially notable because it demonstrates enterprise adoption, not just developer hobbyism. Cloudflare runs the underlying harness against 128 internal repositories continuously, using a six-phase architecture where the agent that finds a vulnerability is never the agent that confirms it.

We tracked the skills marketplace land grab when repos started racing past 250K stars in September. The AAIF donation is not the cause of this adoption — it is the consequence. Anthropic waited for the standard to win, then cemented the win with institutional governance.

The MCP Parallel — and Where It Breaks Down

The comparisons to MCP are obvious. Both started as Anthropic products. Both became open standards. Both landed in the AAIF. But the skills donation is different in one critical way: the security surface is far larger.

MCP connects agents to data sources and tools. A malicious MCP server is dangerous, but the attack requires the user to explicitly connect to it. Skills are different. Skills are markdown files that agents are designed to trust and follow. They load implicitly based on matching context — often without the user choosing them specifically. A skill does not need to trick a firewall or exploit a CVE. It just needs to be in the right folder when the agent starts.

Read the full Snyk ToxicSkills report →

The Snyk ToxicSkills audit in February 2026 quantified the problem: out of 3,984 skills scanned on ClawHub and skills.sh, 76 contained confirmed malicious payloads, 534 (13.4%) had critical-severity issues, and 1,467 (36.82%) had at least one security flaw. The attack patterns are sophisticated — base64-encoded exfiltration targeting AWS credentials, systemctl backdoors, and prompt injection combined with malware in 91% of malicious samples. Three named threat actors (zaycv, Aslaep123, aztr0nutzs) were publishing malicious skills at scale.

The Cloud Security Alliance's CISO Briefing framed it bluntly: "The attack surface is not a code path — it is a document that agents are designed to trust and follow." A separate typosquatting campaign, "clawdhub," targeted 341 skills with reverse shells and data exfiltration payloads aimed at OpenClaw users.

View the OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 →

OWASP responded by creating an entire Agentic Skills Top 10, with AST01 — Malicious Skills — at the top. Their analysis found a separate campaign, ClawHavoc, with 1,184 malicious skills across 12 publisher accounts. The core problem: agent skills execute with the full permissions of the host agent — shell access, API keys, filesystem writes. We analyzed this exact attack surface in our skills supply-chain security deep dive, and the skills-vs-MCP architecture comparison explains why the trust models differ so fundamentally.

Let us be precise about what the AAIF donation does and does not change.

What changes:

  • Spec ownership moves from Anthropic's GitHub org to the AAIF. No single company can unilaterally change the standard.
  • Formal process for spec changes: Anthropic proposed versioned releases and a proposal process (similar to Python PEPs or TC39 for JavaScript).
  • Multi-vendor maintainers: Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and others maintain the standard in their individual capacities — not as corporate delegates.
  • Legitimacy signal for enterprises considering adoption. Foundation governance under the Linux Foundation is the same model that governs Kubernetes, Node.js, and GraphQL.

What does not change:

  • No security framework. The proposed roadmap includes "security guidance" but no mandatory signing, scanning, or audit requirements.
  • No quality gates. The spec defines a format, not a minimum quality bar. The ecosystem benchmarks show the average public skill scores 6.2 out of 12 on quality metrics.
  • No registry governance. Skills.sh has 288K development skills. SkillsMP indexes 1.9 million scraped from GitHub. Neither has security review. The AAIF governs the spec, not the distribution channels.
  • Anthropic's influence. The company that designed the standard, built the reference implementation, and co-founded the foundation will continue to shape its direction. The lead maintainers are Anthropic engineers. This is open governance, not absent governance.

Read the full analysis on Dev.to →

But MCP was already being adopted before the donation, so a foundation home alone does not drive adoption." The same applies here. The standard won on merit — the governance change makes the win durable.

The Ecosystem Right Now: Scale Without Safety

The raw numbers are staggering. The Agent Skills Ecosystem Report maps the current landscape:

Read the full Ecosystem Report →

  • Skills.sh launched in January 2026 and now hosts 288,811 development skills alone, with 86,948 in product management and 74,510 in marketing.
  • SkillsMP indexes 1.9 million skills scraped from public GitHub — no security review.
  • SkillHub offers 7,000+ AI-evaluated skills.
  • Agensi runs a curated marketplace with 8-point security scans and a 70/30 revenue split for creators.
  • Anthropic's official directory remains small and manually curated — quality over quantity.

Roughly 40 products sit on the agentskills.io showcase as of mid-2026, spanning coding agents (Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI), open-source agents (Goose, OpenCode, Amp), and enterprise platforms (Databricks Genie Code, Snowflake Cortex Code). A Digital Applied survey found that 68% of production agent deployments have adopted MCP or an equivalent tool standard. Skills are following the same adoption curve.

But distribution has outpaced security. The gap between "1.9 million indexed skills" and "76 confirmed malicious" is not a safety margin — it is an audit deficit. The confirmed malicious skills were found by Snyk in a sample of just 3,984 out of nearly 2 million. Scale the detection ratio and the number gets concerning fast.

What This Means for Builders

If you are building or shipping agent skills today, the governance change creates a concrete set of implications:

💡 The Practitioner Playbook:

  1. The spec is stable enough to bet on. Foundation governance signals that the SKILL.md format, the YAML metadata schema, and the progressive-loading model are not going to change underneath you. If you have been holding off because the standard was "Anthropic's thing," that objection is gone.

  2. Security is your problem, not the spec's. The AAIF governs the format, not the supply chain. If you install skills from public directories, you need your own vetting process. Snyk's uvx mcp-scan@latest --skills is a starting point. Check our audit landscape analysis for a deeper look at vetting options.

  3. The directory land grab is wide open. With 1.9 million skills indexed and no dominant curated marketplace, the opportunity is in quality, not quantity. Agensi's security-scan-plus-revenue-split model, SkillsBench's quality benchmarks, and Cloudflare's validation approach all point toward the same thesis: curation wins.

  4. Cross-platform is now the default. Skills that only work on one agent are leaving adoption on the table. The spec is implemented by 70+ platforms — design for portability and test on at least three agents before publishing.

  5. Learn the playbook. Anthropic's strategy — build proprietary, prove value, open the standard, donate governance — is the template for setting AI infrastructure standards. If you are building anything that could become a standard (protocols, formats, runtime conventions), this is the path to adoption without getting forked.

The Anthropic Playbook — Why It Keeps Working

Here is what makes Anthropic's approach effective, and why it keeps working:

Lock-in without lock-in. By the time skills reached the AAIF, 70 platforms had already built integrations against Anthropic's specification. Donating governance does not reduce Anthropic's influence — it makes the influence permanent. The spec will evolve under the AAIF, but it will evolve from the foundation Anthropic laid. Every platform that adopted the standard is now building on Anthropic's design decisions.

The MCP precedent removes objections. When MCP was donated to the AAIF in December 2025, skeptics asked whether foundation governance was real or performative. Ten months later, Google's A2A protocol joined as a hosted project, and the AAIF membership grew past 250 organizations including Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg. The foundation has weight. Donating Agent Skills to the same body is a lower-risk bet for everyone involved.

Timing matters. Anthropic did not donate early, when the standard needed credibility. It donated after adoption proved the standard works. The million-skill, 280-million-install numbers are the justification — not the goal — of the donation. This is a victory lap with institutional clothing.

What Comes Next

The proposed roadmap includes versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance. Feedback goes through the project's Discord. Three predictions for the next 12 months:

Prediction 1: Security scanning becomes mandatory in major directories. The Snyk and OWASP findings have made the problem undeniable. Expect Skills.sh and SkillsMP to add at minimum automated scanning — and expect enterprises to require it. The skills standard itself may gain a security metadata field for declaring permissions and data access.

Prediction 2: The AAIF becomes the de facto governance body for the agent infrastructure stack. MCP (data and tools), Agent Skills (capabilities), A2A (inter-agent delegation) — the foundation now hosts all three layers. Whoever proposes the next protocol addition has a clear path: the AAIF.

Prediction 3: Skills specialization accelerates. The scientific skills library pattern was early evidence that domain-specific skills outperform generic ones. With foundation governance signaling long-term stability, expect more vertical investment — legal, medical, financial, compliance — from organizations that were waiting for the standard to settle. The ecosystem already has 382K downloads on some bundles, and the race to own vertical niches is just beginning.

The Agent Skills standard is now infrastructure. It is governed by a foundation, implemented by 70+ platforms, and stress-tested by 280 million installs. Anthropic set the spec, proved it worked, and handed over the keys — to a building it helped design. That is not generosity. That is strategy. And it is the playbook for anyone building the next piece of AI infrastructure.

title: How I Built a Free Hash Generator That Runs 100% in Your Browser
summary:
How I Built a Free Hash Generator That Runs 100% in Your Browser

Every week I add a free tool to toolsofweb.com, and the newest one is a hash generator. It computes MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 — plus HMAC for all of them — without a server, an account, or a single byte of your data leaving the tab.

This isn't a launch post. It's a build log: the decisions I made, the crypto API quirks I hit, and the code that shipped.

Why client-side matters for this one

Most free hash tools online paste your input into a form, POST it to a server, and return the digest. For a hash generator, that's backwards: people hash things precisely because the data is sensitive — passwords before storing them, file checksums before trusting a download, API secrets when debugging HMAC signatures.

The site's rule is simple: anything you hash stays on your machine. The whole tool is a React component plus one TypeScript module, and the only "backend" is crypto.subtle — the WebCrypto API already living in your browser.

MD5: hand-rolled, RFC 1321, streaming

Here's the surprise: browsers no longer ship MD5 in WebCrypto. crypto.subtle.digest() supports SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, but MD5 was left behind because it's not collision-resistant anymore.

Still, people need MD5 constantly — legacy database fields, Gravatar URLs, htpasswd files (our htpasswd generator uses it). So I wrote an incremental MD5 implementation straight from RFC 1321:

export class Md5 {
  private a = 0x67452301; // Initial state, straight from the RFC
  private b = 0xefcdab89;
  private c = 0x98badcfe;
  private d = 0x10325476;
  private buf = new Uint8Array(64); // one 512-bit block
  ...
}

The round constants are derived the way the spec demands — floor(abs(sin(i+1)) * 2^32) — no magic-number tables copied from the internet. And because the class is incremental (update() keeps 64 bytes of internal buffering and processes full blocks as they arrive), I can hash a 100 MB file in chunks without loading it all into memory. That matters on phones.

One detail I was careful about: I verified my implementation byte-for-byte against the MD5 function already powering the site's htpasswd generator. Two implementations agreeing on every test vector means a bug would have to exist identically in both — unlikely. md5("hello") gives the famous 5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592, as expected.

SHA family: let the browser do the heavy lifting

For SHA-1 through SHA-512, there was no reason to hand-roll anything. WebCrypto's digest() is implemented in the browser's native crypto layer — it's faster and better reviewed than anything I'd write:

const digest = await crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', data);

One gotcha worth knowing: crypto.subtle.digest() is async and takes an ArrayBuffer (a bare Uint8Array needs a cast). The tool computes all five digests in parallel with Promise.all for text input, so the UI updates essentially instantly — no loading spinner for normal text.

HMAC: half native, half by hand

The tool has an HMAC tab — you supply a key and a message, it signs it. For HMAC-SHA-*, WebCrypto has you covered:

const cryptoKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
  'raw', keyBuffer, { name: 'HMAC', hash: 'SHA-256' }, false, ['sign']
);
const sig = await crypto.subtle.sign('HMAC', cryptoKey, data);

But HMAC-MD5 needs the hand-rolled MD5 again, built exactly per RFC 2104:

HMAC(K, m) = H((K' ⊕ opad) || H((K' ⊕ ipad) || m))

with ipad = 0x36 and opad = 0x5c repeated over a 64-byte block-sized key (hash the key first if it's longer than 64 bytes). Nothing exotic, but getting the padding exactly right is the whole game with HMAC, so I tested it against Python's hmac module output before shipping.

Four tabs, each answering one real question

The UI is four tabs, one per question people actually ask:

  1. Text — "What are the hashes of this string?" All five digests compute live as you type.
  2. File checksum — "Is this download intact?" Drop a file (up to 100 MB) and it gets hashed locally — FileReader reads the bytes, WebCrypto/MD5 digests them, nothing uploads. Then paste the checksum the publisher listed and use…
  3. Compare — "Does this match?" Paste the expected hash and your input; the tool auto-detects the algorithm from the hex length (32 chars → MD5, 40 → SHA-1, 64 → SHA-256, 96 → SHA-384, 128 → SHA-512) and reports match/mismatch.
  4. HMAC — "What's the signature for this webhook payload?" Key + message → signature.

Real example: after downloading a Linux ISO, the mirror usually publishes a SHA-256 checksum. Open the File checksum tab, drop the ISO, compare against the published value. If it matches, the file wasn't corrupted or tampered with in transit. Doing this without uploading a 3 GB file to someone's server is the entire point of building it client-side.

What I learned shipping this

  • WebCrypto is async everywhere. Mixing it with a synchronous hand-rolled MD5 meant making the MD5 path synchronous and the SHA path async, then joining results with Promise.all. Fine, but plan the API boundary early.
  • Verify against independent implementations. My MD5 cross-checks against the htpasswd generator's MD5; my HMAC-MD5 cross-checks against Python's hmac module. One self-consistent implementation can be self-consistently wrong.
  • Streaming isn't optional for files. A naive implementation reads the whole file into memory. The incremental MD5 processes 64-byte blocks as they arrive; WebCrypto handles its own chunking internally. Keep the memory footprint flat.
  • MD5 is still everywhere. People reach for it for checksums, cache keys, deduplication — non-security uses where collision resistance doesn't matter. A "SHA-only" tool would have missed half the use cases.

Try it

The tool is free, no signup, no ads: toolsofweb.com/hash-generator. Paste some text, drop a file, or check an HMAC — everything happens in your browser, and I never see any of it.

If there's a hash-related feature you'd want (bcrypt/argon2 wrappers, keccak, bulk file hashing), the site has a request-a-tool form — every request gets read.

title: Refund Sloth 🦥: Local AI Agents That Get Your Money Back While You Nap
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Somewhere between 48% and 79% of us have paid for a free trial we forgot to cancel. The average person loses $187–$540 a year to forgotten trials, missed return windows and subscriptions they stopped using. We think we spend about $86 a month on subscriptions; it's closer to $219. And 44% of people keep a subscription simply because cancelling is a chore.

That's the most sloth-shaped problem I know: the money is recoverable, but only if you do boring admin before a deadline.

Refund Sloth 🦥 does the boring part. You drop receipts, order emails and your bank statement into one folder (or let it read your mailbox) and go to sleep. At 2 AM a team of six local AI agents wakes up:

  • 🔭 Scout finds new files through the official filesystem MCP server, locked to the inbox.
  • 📖 Reader reads receipt photos with a vision model, and PDFs and emails with a text model, into strict JSON.
  • 🦅 Deadline Hawk works out return-by, trial-end, warranty and renewal dates and creates calendar reminders.
  • 🧾 Auditor finds recurring charges in your bank CSV and flags 🧟 zombie, 👯 duplicate and 📈 price-hiked subscriptions.
  • 👻 Ghostwriter drafts the cancellation and return emails.
  • 🦥 Sloth Boss reviews everything with tool calls and writes your morning brief.

In the morning you get a notification:

🦥 3 deadlines this week · $86.96/mo you can cut · 10 drafts ready
Most urgent: ⏳ Peacock Premium free trial ends 2026-10-23 ($7.99 at stake).

You open the dashboard, click Approve & copy, paste, send. Or click Cancel now ↗ to jump straight to the store's cancel page. Total effort: about 30 seconds. The sloth never sends or pays anything itself: a human stays in the loop, always.

Even lazier extras:

  • 📬 Connect mail (optional): give it a Gmail, iCloud or Outlook app password and it fetches order, trial and renewal emails by itself. The mailbox is opened read-only, and the password is stored encrypted on your machine (macOS Keychain / Windows DPAPI).
  • 🚨 Urgent popup: anything ending in the next 2 days gets its own desktop notification and a red banner at the top of the dashboard.
  • ↗️ Cancel now: every trial, subscription and return has a button that opens the store's cancel or return page. No more hunting for the hidden cancel link.
  • 🖥️ Runs on macOS and Windows.

Who gets to be lazier? Anyone with a stack of receipts in a drawer, a "free" trial they meant to cancel, and a gym membership they've been "about to use again" since March.

Demo

Today: the urgent banner, the morning brief, and money saved vs. money at risk.

Subscriptions: zombies, duplicates and price hikes, each with a Cancel link.

Action queue: ready-to-send emails. Nothing leaves without your click.

All data in the demo is fake (generated fixtures). No real receipts or bank statements were harmed.

Code

amangithub01 / refund-sloth

🦥 Local AI agents that get your money back while you nap. Open-weight models (Ollama) + MCP, no API keys, no cloud.

🦥 Refund Sloth

Local AI agents that get your money back while you nap. Drop receipts, order emails and bank statements into a folder. Overnight, a team of open-weight models running on your laptop finds forgotten free trials, closing return windows, expiring warranties and zombie subscriptions, then drafts the cancellation and return emails for you. In the morning you click Approve.

No API keys. No cloud. $0 per run. Works with Wi-Fi off.

🎬 Demo

▶️ Full-quality video: docs/media/refund-sloth-demo.mp4 (26 s, demo data, fake "today" = 2026-10-21)

📸 Screenshots

Landing Scroll: the laptop orbit
Today: urgent banner + morning brief Deadlines
Subscriptions: zombies, duplicates, price hikes Action queue: drafts you approve

All data in the demo is fake (eval/fixtures). No real receipts or bank statements are in this repo.

Open http://localhost:4747 for the landing page; the dashboard lives at http://localhost:4747/#today.

Why

  • 48–79% of people have paid…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Every model runs locally through Ollama. No API keys anywhere in the project.

Agent Open-weight model Why
Reader (images) qwen2.5vl:7b small, fast vision model; reads crumpled receipt photos
Reader (text), Hawk, Auditor, Ghostwriter, Boss qwen3.5:35b strong JSON output and tool calling; runs well on an M3 Max
Lite profile qwen3:8b + qwen2.5vl:3b for laptops with 8–16 GB of RAM

MCP is the backbone. I wrote five small MCP servers in TypeScript over stdio:

  • ledger (SQLite)
  • docs (PDF, image, EML, MBOX and CSV parsing)
  • calendar (.ics files with alarms)
  • notify (desktop notifications and the brief)
  • mail (read-only IMAP)

Alongside them runs the official @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem, rooted at the inbox with only its read-only tools exposed. A small harness (McpHub) starts every server, turns their tools into Ollama tool definitions and runs the agent loops. The full architecture diagram is in the README.

Hybrid by design: rules for math, models for mess. The biggest lesson: don't let an LLM do arithmetic on your money.

  • Plain code: hashing and dedup, all deadline math (document date, then policies.json, then a clearly marked AI guess), recurring-charge detection, the zombie, duplicate and price-hike flags, and every number in the brief. All unit-tested.
  • LLMs: reading messy documents, guessing return policies for unknown stores, naming bank descriptors (APPLE.COM/BILL 866-712-7753 CA → "Apple Music"), writing emails, and the Boss's review.

Structured output that doesn't break. Every LLM call uses a zod schema, converted to JSON Schema and passed to Ollama's format, then validated. On failure it retries with the validation error. Low-confidence extractions go to a "🔎 Needs a look" list instead of being silently wrong.

A lesson from the local models: prompt-only email formatting was ignored (one-line bodies, greeting the wrong company). Moving layout into deterministic post-processing fixed all of it. Small models are great at content; let code handle form.

Eval. sloth eval runs the full pipeline on fake fixtures: receipt photos, PDF invoices, order emails, an mbox, a 13-month bank CSV, and a meme that must be ignored.

Metric Score
Field accuracy (merchant / amount / date) 96.7% (29/30)
Deadline accuracy (type + date ±1 day) 100% (14/14)
Subscription recall / flag accuracy 100% / 100%
False positives 0 (the meme is correctly ignored)
Time ~3 minutes for the whole batch, fully local (M3 Max, 48 GB)

Stack: TypeScript, Node 24 (built-in node:sqlite), MCP TypeScript SDK, Ollama JS, zod, imapflow, Express 5 + SSE (a live agent log), React 19 + Vite + Tailwind v4, Vitest (39 tests).

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this project it isn't a nice-to-have. It's the only way the project can exist.

  • Privacy. To find a forgotten trial you need someone's bank statement, receipts and order emails: their whole financial life. With a closed API, that's a nightly upload of your bank CSV to someone else's server. With open weights it never leaves the laptop. sloth doctor even fails if Ollama isn't on localhost, and the dashboard API only listens on 127.0.0.1.
  • Works offline. Nothing in the pipeline needs the internet; try it with Wi-Fi off. A 2 AM job shouldn't depend on a connection or an API being up.
  • $0 per run, forever. It runs every night. A closed API would charge per token, every night, to save me money. Ironic.
  • Swappable. Each agent's model is one line in a config. I switch between a 35B model and an 8B "lite" profile, and a single profile uses one multimodal model for everything. No vendor lock-in, and no deprecation can break my nightly job.

title: Agent Skills Moves to the Agentic AI Foundation: What Developers Need to Know
summary:
Short answer: Anthropic donated the Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation on October 22, 2026. This transfer places the skill specification under neutral Linux Foundation governance alongside the Model Context Protocol. Developers can build skills using simple local directories, Markdown instructions, and executable scripts, then run them across dozens of supported agent clients and model backends without encountering platform lock-in.

What did Anthropic donate on October 22?

On October 22, 2026, Anthropic transferred the Agent Skills standard and all related assets to the Agentic AI Foundation. The donation includes the core specification, the Agent Skills name and logo, the official GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. Anthropic stated that it is committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral.

The Agentic AI Foundation operates as a project under the Linux Foundation to host vendor-neutral agent standards. Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI co-founded the foundation in 2025 to create a shared home for open agent infrastructure. The foundation already hosts the Model Context Protocol, which Anthropic donated in an earlier governance transfer.

Anthropic first launched Agent Skills inside its Claude products in October 2025. Two months later, in December 2025, Anthropic published the underlying format as an open standard for the developer community. Donating the assets to the Agentic AI Foundation completes the transition from a single-vendor feature to a neutral industry specification.

Who maintains Agent Skills now?

Two Lead Maintainers, David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag, now guide the Agent Skills project. Individual software engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other technology companies maintain the specification on their own behalf rather than through corporate representation.

Development teams do not need to join the Agentic AI Foundation to use the standard or contribute code to the repository.

Anyone who wants to suggest changes to the specification can send feedback through the project's Discord server.

How widely is the standard used?

More than 70 agent platforms have integrated the Agent Skills specification across their production tools. That adoption footprint includes major coding agents and developer environments such as ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code.

According to Anthropic, developers have published 1 million skills and end users have installed nearly 280 million skills across those integrated platforms. These are Anthropic's own figures and are not independently audited.

For skill authors, that means one package format across competing platforms. Developers who author a skill can deploy that package directly to multiple editors and command-line agents without rewriting instructions for each client.

What is inside a skill?

A skill is a directory containing at minimum a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter followed by standard Markdown instructions. The directory can also house optional subdirectories by convention, including scripts for executable code, references for documentation loaded on demand, and assets for templates, images, or data files.

api-cost-check/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   └── estimate.py
└── references/
    └── prices.md

File references inside SKILL.md should be relative paths from the skill root, kept one level deep. The specification advises against long chains of nested references.

The YAML frontmatter defines two required fields: name and description. The name field takes a string between 1 and 64 characters containing only lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens. It must match the parent directory name exactly, with no leading hyphens, trailing hyphens, or double hyphens.

The description field accepts 1 to 1,024 characters explaining what the skill accomplishes and when the agent should select it. Authors should write clear descriptions with relevant keywords, because the agent runtime inspects this text to decide which skill fits a given user prompt.

Frontmatter also supports four optional fields. The license field names the distribution license, while compatibility accepts up to 500 characters outlining environment requirements. Authors can provide arbitrary string key-value pairs through the metadata map, or specify an experimental allowed-tools list containing space-separated pre-approved tools.

---
name: api-cost-check
description: "Estimates the API cost of a prompt or batch job before it runs. Use when the user asks what a request, batch or agent run will cost on a given model."
license: Apache-2.0
metadata:
  author: example-org
  version: "1.0"
---

# API cost check

1. Count input tokens and estimate output tokens.
2. Read per-1M-token prices from references/prices.md.
3. Run scripts/estimate.py and report the cost per request and per 1,000 requests.

Developers can verify their directory structure and schema formatting before distributing a package. Running skills-ref validate ./my-skill through the skills-ref reference library checks that the frontmatter is valid and follows the naming rules.

How does progressive disclosure keep context small?

Roughly 100 tokens of metadata per skill enter the context window when an agent session initializes. The runtime loads only the name and description fields at startup, allowing an agent to index dozens of capabilities without consuming substantial context space.

The agent defers reading the rest of the package until the user prompt triggers that specific skill. The full body of SKILL.md loads into the active prompt only upon activation, and the specification recommends keeping that body under 5,000 tokens and under 500 lines of text.

Files located inside the scripts, references, and assets subdirectories remain unloaded until the activated instructions specifically call for them. This phased approach prevents large documentation files and scripts from bloating context during unrelated prompts.

Fifty installed skills add about 5,000 tokens of metadata at session start. At an input price of $2 per 1M tokens before prompt caching, loading metadata for all 50 skills costs roughly $0.01 per session.

How are skills different from MCP?

The Model Context Protocol connects an agent to external tools and live data stores through client-server connections. In contrast, an Agent Skill packages procedural instructions, executable scripts, and static reference files that an agent runtime reads directly from disk.

MCP relies on active server processes that expose tool definitions, resources, and prompt templates over standard communication protocols. A skill functions as a static file bundle that informs the model how to complete a specific task using tools already available on the host.

Both standards now operate under the Agentic AI Foundation as complementary building blocks. A skill can direct an agent on when and how to call an MCP server, while the MCP server handles the protocol communication with remote systems.

What is on the roadmap, and why does security matter?

The proposed starting roadmap for Agent Skills focuses on three areas: versioned releases, a formal specification proposal process, and security guidance for authors and users. A structured release cycle will help tool builders maintain compatibility as the format matures under foundation governance.

Security guidance represents an immediate priority because a skill can include arbitrary code in its scripts directory. When a skill's instructions tell the agent to run those scripts, they run with whatever access the agent has on that machine.

Installing a skill therefore means trusting the author who packaged it. Malicious or poorly tested scripts can modify local files, execute dangerous shell commands, or expose sensitive project data. Developers should always review the contents of the scripts directory before installing third-party skills into their environments.

How do you use skills with any model through one API key?

Claude Code reads personal skills from ~/.claude/skills//SKILL.md and project-level skills from .claude/skills//SKILL.md inside the root of a repository.

Skills are plain text files evaluated by the agent client rather than the upstream model provider. Because the client parses the frontmatter and passes the instructions to the model, the same skill files work whichever model the client calls, although results still depend on the model.

Developers can run Claude Code through the Tokely API gateway by setting two environment variables. The skill directories stay exactly as they are.

skills-ref validate ./api-cost-check
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.tokely.me ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN='' claude

A single Tokely API key and unified balance grants access to Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Kimi models, including Kimi K3.1 Pro. The gateway exposes an Anthropic-compatible endpoint for Claude Code and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for other agent clients, so a team can test the same skill on several models from one account. You can view all supported options on the Tokely models page or read our guide on using Claude Code with a cheaper API.

Sources

Read the announcement details at Anthropic's announcement and explore technical definitions in the Agent Skills specification. Further context appears in Simon Willison's note and our setup tutorial for Claude Code with a cheaper API.

title: The Cloud Is Now Optional: Inside the Offline AI Stack You Can Actually Run Today
summary:
Offline AI is genuinely usable today for chat, coding and voice — here is the stack, the hardware tiers, and the honest limits.

For three years, the assumption was simple: serious AI lives in someone else's data center, and you rent it by the token. This week that assumption cracked. A voice stack that runs entirely on cheap Android phones, a 428B open-weights model you can download, a PIN lock on ChatGPT, and a new encrypted assistant all landed within about 48 hours — different products, same direction. The cloud did not disappear. It became a choice. We researched the announcements, the specs and the reporting to work out what you can actually run today, where the limits still bite, and who should bother.

How we put this together: We reviewed vendor announcements and launch-week coverage for VoxNexus VoxEdge and VoxSense, OpenAI's ChatGPT PIN lock and Dark.ai, plus Nasscom's India Voice AI Readiness 2026 report and MiniMax's M3.1 Flash release. Specs and figures are quoted from those sources; where a vendor makes a performance claim we have not seen independently reproduced, we label it as a vendor claim. We have not hands-on tested these systems — this is researched analysis based on specs and reporting, not a lab test.

Verdict: Offline AI is genuinely usable today for chat, coding assistance and voice — not as a stunt, but as a daily driver for a lot of work. Small and mid-size open-weights models run well on a normal laptop, voice recognition and synthesis can now live entirely on a phone, and the tooling has gone from hobbyist to install-and-go. The limits are real at the frontier end: the smartest models, the longest contexts and the hardest reasoning still live in the cloud, and at the extreme a single downloadable model can need 220GB just to sit on disk. Start local for privacy, cost and speed on routine tasks. Keep the cloud for the jobs that actually need it.

What changed this week

Start in Madrid. On October 23, 2026, VoxNexus unveiled VoxEdge: a full voice AI stack designed to run entirely offline on cheap Android phones. Speech recognition in 36 languages, translation in 103 languages, speech synthesis in 45 languages — with no connection required and, in the pitch that matters to businesses, zero per-token cloud bills.

The detail that got engineers' attention was size. VoxEdge's speech recognition model is just 65 million parameters, and VoxNexus claims — vendor claim, not independently verified — that it beats open models ten times its size. Whether that claim survives independent testing matters, but the direction does not: models are getting small enough that "phone-grade" no longer means "toy-grade."

Alongside it came VoxSense, an always-on listening layer. VoxNexus says it can listen for 12 hours on 2.49% battery — again, a vendor figure — with audio never uploaded. That last part is the product. Always-on listening is only acceptable to most people if the recording never leaves the device.

title: Why I Built Nathstar: A Local-First, 120Hz Native macOS Terminal for Projects, Live Ops & Private AI
summary:
If you are a developer on macOS today, picking a terminal emulator feels like a forced compromise:

  1. Minimalist GPU Emulators (Ghostty, Alacritty, Kitty): Blazingly fast and standards-compliant, but they treat every window as an isolated, stateless text grid. When you're juggling four microservices, two SSH sessions, and a CLI coding agent, they have no idea which pane is holding port :3000 hostage, which background build failed ten minutes ago, or which .env variables are loaded.
  2. Cloud-Tethered "Block" Terminals (Warp): Great input editing and AI features, but built around cloud accounts, telemetry by default, and metered subscriptions—while replacing standard terminal buffers with custom UI layers that can fight full-screen TUIs like nvim, lazygit, or htop.

I wanted both worlds without the trade-offs.

So I built Nathstar — an open-source (MIT), 100% local-first, zero-telemetry macOS terminal written in Swift 6, SwiftUI, AppKit, and Metal.

Here is a look at what Nathstar does differently and the engineering under the hood.

1. Projects Over Windows: Persistent Workspaces

Traditional terminals organize your work by disposable windows and tabs. When you return to a project after a reboot or context switch, you're left reconstructing your layout from shell history and memory.

In Nathstar, the primary unit of organization is a Project Workspace:

  • Categorized & Collapsible Sidebar: Organize repositories into Projects, Personal, and Others, plus an auto-discovered SSH Hosts section parsed directly from ~/.ssh/config. You can rename sections, drag-and-drop workspaces between them, or unpin the sidebar into an auto-expanding 44pt hover rail (⇧⌘S).
  • Recursive Split Panes & Zoom: Split panes vertically (⌘D) or horizontally (⇧⌘D), equalize ratios (⇧⌘=), or temporarily maximize a single pane (⇧⌘⏎).
  • True Single-Window Persistence (⌘W vs. ⌘Q): Closing the window with ⌘W hides the UI while keeping every PTY process, dev server, and SSH connection alive in memory. Double-tapping ⌃ (Control) summons Nathstar back from any app—or docks it to the top of your screen in Quake Visor Mode.

2. Silent Live Environment Sync (SIGUSR1) & .env Management

Have you ever updated an API key or feature flag in a .env file, only to realize you have to restart your shell—or paste export FOO=bar across five open panes—for it to take effect?

Nathstar introduces Silent Live Environment Injection:

  1. When Nathstar spawns zsh, it uses a lightweight, transparent ZDOTDIR shim that sources your real .zshenv and .zshrc untouched and installs a TRAPUSR1 signal handler.
  2. When you add or edit a KEY=VALUE variable in Nathstar's Manifest panel and click Set & Apply, Nathstar writes a private 0600 session file and sends SIGUSR1 (kill(shellPid, SIGUSR1)) to the running zsh process.
  3. Your live shell immediately sources the updated environment variables silently in the background—with zero commands echoed into your scrollback buffer.

You can also import/export .env files with one click, and define a .nathstar/manifest.json file to orchestrate multi-pane project startups (while automatically keeping *_KEY, *_SECRET, and *_TOKEN values strictly local).

3. Who Is Using :3000? Built-In Live Port & Process Manager (⇧⌘P)

Every full-stack developer knows the pain of EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000, followed by running lsof -ti :3000 | xargs kill -9.

Nathstar includes a dedicated Live Ports & Processes (⇧⌘P) tab in the right-hand panel:

  • Every 3 seconds (while open), LivePortScanner inspects listening TCP sockets (lsof) and walks the parent PID (ppid) tree (ps) up to the root shellPid of every Nathstar pane.
  • It maps every active port (:3000, :5173, :8080) back to the exact Workspace and Terminal Pane that spawned it.
  • With a single click, you can Open the port in your browser, Focus the exact terminal pane running the server, send a graceful Kill (SIGTERM), or Kill -9 (SIGKILL) a stuck process.

4. Native Command Editing (⌘E), Click-to-Cursor & Blast-Radius Safety

Editing a 200-character curl or docker command in a traditional terminal usually means holding down the Left arrow key or memorizing readline chords.

Nathstar gives you two ways to edit long commands naturally:

  1. Click-to-Position Cursor in the Prompt: Click (or ⌥-Click) directly on any character in your active terminal command—even across multi-line wrapped lines. Using a hybrid of OSC 133 semantic prompt markers and automatic wrapped-line cell calculation (compatible with Powerlevel10k, Starship, and Oh My Zsh), Nathstar moves the shell cursor straight to that character.
  2. Pull to Native Composer (⌘E): Press ⌘E at any time to pull your active terminal line into the bottom multi-line macOS text editor. Edit with standard macOS selection and undo, use Tab ⇥ IDE-style autocomplete (ranking Git branches, file paths, command history, and {{parameterized}} snippets), and press ⇧⏎ to insert it back into the prompt or ⌘⏎ to run it.

Pre-Execution Blast-Radius Analyzer (Safe-Run)

Before executing commands from the composer, CommandRiskAnalyzer checks for destructive patterns—like git push --force, rm -rf near / or ~, git reset --hard, or piping curl directly into sudo bash—and warns you of the blast radius before execution.

5. Zero-Telemetry Streaming AI (Local Ollama + BYOK Cloud)

AI in the terminal shouldn't require a monthly SaaS subscription or sending proprietary stack traces to someone else's cloud.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro API Pricing: Half of Claude Opus 5.5, Same as Sonnet 5.5
summary:
Short answer: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro at $2 per 1M input tokens and $10 per 1M output tokens. That matches Claude Sonnet 5.5 and cuts Claude Opus 5.5 pricing in half. For long prompts without tiered pricing penalties, Kimi K3.1 Pro provides 1,048,576 tokens of context at a flat rate, alongside a 2 to 3 times faster Highspeed tier at double the price.

What did Moonshot release on October 23?

Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026, as the first model of its K3.1 series. It is a post-trained successor to Kimi K3, which Moonshot released on July 16, 2026, as a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model. Moonshot announced that the full model weights for K3.1 Pro will be released by November 4, 2026.

The release includes two API model IDs: kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Moonshot removed cyber-attack material from training before the open release. On Moonshot's own benchmark, Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 65.7% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, compared to 66.4% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2% for GPT-6 Astra. These benchmark numbers are Moonshot's own and not independently verified, and price is not capability, so test on your own prompts.

How much does Kimi K3.1 Pro cost?

Kimi K3.1 Pro costs $2 per 1M input tokens on cache misses, $0.20 per 1M cached input tokens on cache hits, and $10 per 1M output tokens. Its predecessor, Kimi K3, lists at $3 per 1M input tokens, $0.30 per 1M cached input tokens, and $15 per 1M output tokens, making K3.1 Pro one third cheaper than the model it replaces.

The faster variant, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, lists at $4 per 1M input tokens, $0.20 per 1M cached input tokens, and $20 per 1M output tokens. Cache writes for both models are billed separately by time to live for either 5 minutes or 1 hour. The Vercel AI Gateway lists the cache write fee at $2 per 1M tokens for K3.1 Pro and $4 per 1M tokens for Highspeed.

Moonshot uses flat pay-as-you-go pricing across the entire 1,048,576-token context window. There are no price tiers or rate increases as context lengths scale up toward the one-million-token limit. Direct access on Moonshot's platform requires a top-up of at least $1, and top-up totals determine your rate-limit tier.

How does it compare with Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon?

Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens, exactly double the standard rates of Kimi K3.1 Pro. Claude Sonnet 5.5 matches Kimi K3.1 Pro at $2 per 1M input tokens and $10 per 1M output tokens. Anthropic bills the full 1M-token context window at standard rates for both models, with cache hits at $0.20 for Opus 5.5 and $0.10 for Sonnet 5.5, and cache writes at $5 or $8 for Opus 5.5 and $2.50 or $4 for Sonnet 5.5.

GPT-6.1 Sol lists at $2 per 1M input tokens, $0.10 per 1M cached tokens, and $10 per 1M output tokens for requests up to 272K input tokens. Above 272K input tokens, GPT-6.1 Sol shifts to $4 per 1M input tokens, $0.20 per 1M cached tokens, and $15 per 1M output tokens. Gemini 4 Argon lists at $2 per 1M input tokens, $10 per 1M output tokens, and $0.10 per 1M cached tokens until November 30, 2026, after which it lists at $4 per 1M input tokens, $20 per 1M output tokens, and $0.20 per 1M cached tokens starting December 1, 2026.

Workload A shows the cost of 1M input tokens and 250K output tokens at list prices. On this workload, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Argon (until November 30) all total $4.50. Kimi K3 totals $6.75, while Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed both cost $9.00.


Cost of 1M input plus 250K output tokens at official standard list prices, checked October 24, 2026. Price is not capability: test on your own prompts.

Which model is cheapest for long prompts?

Workload B measures a single long-context request with 500K input tokens and 20K output tokens. For this request, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon (until November 30) each cost $1.20. In contrast, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2.30 because its higher rate tier applies above 272K tokens, while Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed each cost $2.40.


Cost of one request with 500K input plus 20K output tokens. Kimi K3.1 Pro, Claude and Gemini 4 Argon keep one rate across the window; GPT-6.1 Sol bills requests above 272K input tokens at its long-context rate.

Caching economics introduce a specific divergence for repetitive workloads. Cached input on K3.1 Pro costs $0.20 per 1M tokens, which is 10% of its base input price. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol charge $0.10 per 1M cached tokens, cutting cache hit costs in half relative to Moonshot.

That difference changes the ranking for agent loops that reuse long prefixes. If a team runs deep multi-turn sessions where the same system instructions or documents are cached again and again, Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol charge less per cached token than Kimi K3.1 Pro, even though all three share the same $2 base input price.

When is Highspeed worth twice the price?

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is the same model served at 2 to 3 times the generation speed for $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens. That doubling in token pricing directly matches the price tag of Claude Opus 5.5. On a 1M input and 250K output workload, Highspeed reaches $9.00 compared to $4.50 on the standard tier.

This pricing premium pays off specifically when latency dictates system success. Interactive developer tools, synchronous code completion, and customer-facing interfaces benefit from cutting generation times by half or more. Moonshot keeps the cache hit price identical across both tiers at $0.20 per 1M tokens, but cache writes cost $4 per 1M tokens on Highspeed compared to $2 on K3.1 Pro.

For asynchronous workflows like offline evaluation, data extraction, or night-time batch processing, the standard Kimi K3.1 Pro model provides identical quality at half the price. Engineering teams should measure whether user drop-off or task timeouts justify paying double for token throughput before setting Highspeed as the default endpoint.

What do you need to change in your code?

Moonshot's K3.1 Pro quickstart defines several fixed parameters that must be omitted from API requests. The API locks temperature to 1.0, top_p to 0.95, n to 1, presence_penalty to 0, and frequency_penalty to 0. Moonshot asks callers to leave them out of every request.

Thinking is always turned on in K3.1 Pro and cannot be disabled. The reasoning_effort parameter accepts low, high, and max, with max set as the default. Moonshot suggests setting reasoning_effort to low to cut reasoning time.

Handling multi-turn conversations and tool calling requires strict message preservation. In multi-turn and tool-call flows, applications must send the complete assistant message back unchanged in subsequent turns.

Output token caps are flexible across the full million-token window. The max_completion_tokens parameter defaults to 131,072 and can be configured up to 1,048,576. For multimodal requests, images must be submitted as base64 data URLs or uploaded file IDs, as public image URLs are not accepted. Moonshot also notes that its built-in web search is being updated and is not recommended for production workloads for now.

What happens to Kimi K2 models?

Moonshot is phasing out its previous generation of models according to a published timeline. From October 31, 2026, Kimi K2 series models are no longer available to newly registered users on Moonshot's platform. Existing users are not affected by that change.

Moonshot plans to retire all K2 series models entirely by the end of December 2026. Moonshot recommends migrating K2 traffic to Kimi K3.1 Pro. Teams already on Kimi K3 also save a third by moving: $2 per 1M input tokens and $10 per 1M output tokens instead of $3 and $15.

How do you use Kimi K3.1 Pro with one API key?

Tokely lists Kimi K3.1 Pro at Moonshot's list price of $2 per 1M input tokens, $10 per 1M output tokens, and $0.20 per 1M cached tokens. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is also available at list price for $4 per 1M input tokens, $20 per 1M output tokens, and $0.20 per 1M cached tokens. The gateway provides access through an OpenAI-compatible interface, allowing developers to switch models by updating the model identifier.

A single Tokely account, API key, and credit balance connects to Kimi K3.1 Pro alongside Western flagship models. On Tokely, Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $3 per 1M input and $15 per 1M output tokens, Claude Sonnet 5.5 lists at $1.50 per 1M input and $7.50 per 1M output tokens, GPT-6.1 Sol lists at $0.80 per 1M input and $4 per 1M output tokens, and Gemini 4 Argon lists at $1.40 per 1M input and $7 per 1M output tokens. Tokely prices can change, and developers should check the Tokely models page for current rates.

Testing model variations side by side requires no custom client code. The Tokely Playground allows teams to run the same prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro and competing flagship models simultaneously to evaluate speed, reasoning depth, and formatting. You can call Kimi K3.1 Pro on Tokely with the standard OpenAI Python SDK using the following snippet:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.tokely.me/v1", api_key="YOUR_TOKELY_API_KEY")
reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k3.1-pro",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review this function for race conditions."}],
    max_tokens=4096,
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)

Sources

Prices, parameters and migration dates come from the developers' documentation, checked on October 24, 2026; the Highspeed cache write price comes from the Vercel AI Gateway model list. Review implementation details in the Kimi K3.1 Pro quickstart and examine current rates on the Kimi API pricing page. Compare these figures with Western flagship documentation via Claude pricing, OpenAI API pricing, and Gemini API pricing. For background on training data filtering and the open release schedule, read The Next Web on the release. For extended context cost evaluations, consult our earlier comparison Gemini 4 Argon Pricing vs Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol.

title: Give your AI agent SEC EDGAR data: a free remote MCP server for insider trades and XBRL financials
summary:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI client such as Claude, Cursor or VS Code call external tools through one common interface.

This post walks through a free, MIT-licensed MCP server for U.S. SEC EDGAR data. It runs remotely, so there's nothing to install and no API key. I'll show how to connect it, three real calls with their actual output, how it works inside, and where it falls short.

  • Endpoint (Streamable HTTP, no key): https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp
  • Source: https://github.com/monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp-remote
  • MCP Registry name: io.github.monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp

Why EDGAR needs a wrapper

EDGAR is one of the best free financial datasets around: every insider trade, 10-K, 8-K and XBRL financial fact that U.S. public companies file. It's also awkward to use, especially for an agent:

  1. The User-Agent rule. SEC's fair-access policy asks every client to send a declared User-Agent with a contact email and to stay under 10 requests per second. Requests that skip this get 403s. An LLM making fetches on its own won't know that.
  2. CIK lookup. Most endpoints want a 10-digit Central Index Key (0000320193), not a ticker (AAPL). You have to look it up in a roughly 1 MB company_tickers.json file first.
  3. Form 4 is XML. Insider trades come as one XML document per filing, full of transaction codes (P, S, A, M, F, G), derivative tables and footnotes.
  4. XBRL is messy. The companyconcept JSON repeats the same period across many filings and mixes 3-month, 9-month and 12-month durations. Getting "net income by fiscal year" out of it means filtering and de-duplicating.

The server does all of this and returns compact JSON.

The seven tools

Tool What it returns
get_insider_trades Form 4 transactions for a company or an insider, with buy/sell totals and a 10b5-1 flag
get_market_insider_buys Open-market insider purchases across the market, grouped by company, with cluster-buy detection (2+ insiders)
get_company_filings Latest 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K (with item numbers) and other filings, with document links
get_company_snapshot Revenue, margins, net income, EPS, cash flow, balance sheet and YoY growth from XBRL
get_company_concept Annual or quarterly history of any XBRL tag
search_filings EDGAR full-text search with phrase, form and date filters
resolve_company Ticker â†” CIK lookup

Every tool takes a ticker or a CIK, and all of them are marked read-only.

Connect a client

Cursor: add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or .cursor/mcp.json in a project):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sec-edgar": {
      "url": "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp"
    }
  }
}

VS Code (Copilot agent mode): add this to .vscode/mcp.json:

{
  "servers": {
    "sec-edgar": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Claude Desktop: on plans that support custom connectors, add the URL under Settings â†’ Connectors. You can also bridge it through claude_desktop_config.json with the mcp-remote package (needs Node.js):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sec-edgar": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

The server is stateless, so you don't need an SDK to test it. Every request is a single JSON-RPC POST. Start with initialize:

URL=https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp
curl -s $URL \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}}'

1. NVIDIA insider trades
