  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_insider_trades","arguments":{"ticker_or_cik":"NVDA","filings":5,"max_rows":5}}}'

{
 "company": {"id": "NVDA", "cik": "0001045810", "ticker": "NVDA", "name": "NVIDIA CORP"},
 "filingsParsed": 5,
 "summary": {"transactions": 8, "openMarketBuys": 0, "openMarketSells": 5,
             "sellShares": 1396460, "sellValueUsd": 306933627.99, "distinctInsiders": 5},
 "returned": 5,

  {"date": "2026-09-21", "insider": "Teter Timothy S.", "role": "EVP, General Counsel and Sec",
   "code": "S", "shares": 12483, "price": 222.1932, "valueUsd": 2773637.72,
   "ownedAfter": 2705637, "plan10b51": true, "filed": "2026-09-23",
   "url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000169684126000014/wk-form4_1790196985.xml"},
  ...

  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_company_concept","arguments":{"ticker_or_cik":"AAPL","concept":"NetIncomeLoss","period":"annual","limit":4}}}'

  {"value": 93736000000,  "start": "2023-10-01", "end": "2024-09-28", "fy": 2025, "form": "10-K", "filed": "2025-10-31"},
  {"value": 96995000000,  "start": "2022-09-25", "end": "2023-09-30", "fy": 2025, "form": "10-K", "filed": "2025-10-31"},
  ...
 ]
}

3. Cluster buys across the market 

curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_market_insider_buys","arguments":{"days":7,"min_insiders":2,"limit":3}}}'

{
 "window": {"days": 7, "from": "2026-10-17", "to": "2026-10-24"},
 "dataUpdatedAt": "2026-10-24T04:40:38.877Z",
 "issuers": 3, "clusterBuys": 3,
 "results": [
  {"ticker": "RAPP", "issuer": "Rapport Therapeutics, Inc.", "insiderCount": 6, "clusterBuy": true,
   "totalValueUsd": 1664824.35, "totalShares": 61694, "avgPrice": 26.9852,
   "firstDate": "2026-10-21", "lastDate": "2026-10-23",
   "insiders": [{"name": "Ignelzi Troy A.", "role": "Chief Financial Officer", "valueUsd": 143550}, ...]},
  {"ticker": "CHCO", "issuer": "CITY HOLDING CO", "insiderCount": 4, "totalValueUsd": 68222.4, ...},
  {"ticker": "RENT", "issuer": "Rent the Runway, Inc.", "insiderCount": 3, "totalValueUsd": 6120515.95, ...}
 ],
 "note": "Open-market, non-derivative purchases only. Not investment advice."
}

This call made zero SEC requests because it reads from a pre-built store (more on that below). Dates are UTC, which is why the window ends on the 24th.

How it works

The whole thing is one Cloudflare Worker on the free plan:

  • MCP transport. /mcp uses the official MCP TypeScript SDK's web-standard Streamable HTTP transport in stateless JSON mode. There are no sessions and no Durable Object per client. Each POST stands alone, and GET/DELETE return 405. Each tool maps to one REST endpoint, and a compact() function trims the REST JSON down to fewer fields and capped rows so it doesn't fill the model's context. The same Worker also serves that REST API (/v1/..., documented in openapi.yaml).
  • SEC etiquette. Every request to SEC carries a declared User-Agent with a contact email. Requests are spaced at least 115 ms apart, and a global Durable Object rate limiter hands out time slots so that all Worker isolates together stay near 8.7 req/s, under SEC's 10 req/s ceiling. On 429/5xx the Worker backs off (honoring Retry-After) and retries up to three times. A 403 gets one retry and then a clear error.
  • Caching. Lookups go through three layers: isolate memory, then the Cloudflare Cache API, then KV for selected keys. TTLs follow how often the data changes. The ticker map and resolutions are cached for 24 h, parsed Form 4s for 30 days (filings don't change), submissions for 10 min, XBRL snapshots and concepts for 6 h, and full-text search for 15 min.
  • Market-wide buys. A cron runs every 10 minutes. It queries EDGAR full-text search for new Form 4s, parses up to 40 per run, and keeps open-market purchases (code P, non-derivative) in a KV store. get_market_insider_buys groups that store by issuer.
  • Ticker resolution. The ticker file is searched with a regex instead of JSON.parse, which keeps it inside the free plan's CPU budget.

Limits and caveats

  • Shallow per-call history. get_insider_trades parses at most 25 recent Form 4 filings per call (default 5). The free plan allows about 50 subrequests per invocation, so this isn't a tool for pulling ten years of history.
  • Market scan coverage. The cluster-buy data covers at most 30 days and only starts from when the store was first populated. During a burst of filings the cron can fall behind.
  • XBRL is only as clean as the filings. Companies choose different tags (Revenues vs. RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax), and some metrics will come back null. Check the tag field in the snapshot.
  • Shared free endpoint. The public instance has no key and no SLA. Under heavy load you'll queue behind the global SEC limit or get a 503 asking you to retry. For anything important, deploy your own copy (the README covers it: a KV namespace, your own SEC_USER_AGENT, then wrangler deploy). You can protect /mcp with MCP_API_KEYS.
  • Not investment advice, not affiliated with the SEC. The data is public domain and comes straight from EDGAR. Interpreting it is up to you. A 10b5-1 sale means something very different from a discretionary open-market buy.

Links

  • Source code (MIT): https://github.com/monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp-remote
  • For scheduled or bulk Form 4 pulls outside an agent loop, there's an Apify actor: https://apify.com/monriah-studio/sec-form4-insider-trades

Issues and pull requests are welcome on the repo.

Written with AI assistance and checked by a human.

title: From ImportError to Video: Bringing Looking Ahead to Windows
summary:
Looking Ahead's 1.3B image-to-video example stopped on my Windows machine before inference started:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fcntl'

The machine had an RTX 5090. FlashAttention 4 was installed. Neither was enough to get past the import.

My fix, TencentARC/Looking-Ahead PR #2, was merged on October 23, 2026 (UTC). With the patch, the tested 1.3B example produced 80 frames at 768×432 on Windows 11, using PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention fallback.

The change spans six files. The interesting part is how three separate assumptions had to be removed before the fallback actually worked end to end.

Why I wanted to run Looking Ahead

Looking Ahead is a video-generation research project from researchers at Nanjing University, Tencent ARC Lab, and Zhejiang University.

Its method, Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), addresses a shortcut in autoregressive video training: neighboring video chunks can be similar enough that a model relies on local continuity without learning much about how a scene evolves.

FCP adds auxiliary training branches that predict more distant future chunks from the current chunk's intermediate features, without seeing the intervening chunks. Those branches are removed at inference. The authors report improvements in physical consistency; the project page explains the method and shows their comparisons.

The released code includes 1.3B and 5B models. Its documented test environment was Linux with an NVIDIA H200. My contribution makes the tested Windows inference path accessible through the upstream code. It does not change FCP, retrain the model, or establish Windows support for every configuration.

That is why this merge matters to me: the compatibility fix now lives in the research repository, where the next person trying the model can receive it.

1. Installed does not mean importable

The attention modules used is_flash_attn_4_available() before importing flash_attn.cute.

In the tested environment, that availability check reported the installed package. Importing it still failed: its quack dependency imported fcntl, a Unix-specific module unavailable on Windows.

The merged code attempts the import and treats an ImportError as an unavailable optional backend:

FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE = is_flash_attn_4_available()
if FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE:
    try:
        import flash_attn.cute
    except ImportError as exc:
        FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE = False
        warn_flash_attention_fallback(type(exc).__name__, str(exc))

Both attention modules receive this handling. A shared helper logs the selected backend and reports each distinct import failure once.

The warning explicitly says that performance and numerical results may differ. That matters because a run that silently switches backend is harder to reproduce or compare.

The helper receives the exception type and message as strings. It does not cache the exception object and its traceback just to deduplicate a warning.

This check establishes importability, not a guarantee that every subsequent kernel call will work on every device. It also catches ImportError specifically; it does not convert arbitrary runtime failures into silent fallbacks.

2. Cross-attention bypassed the fallback

Getting past the import exposed the next problem.

The code already had an attention() function that selected between FlashAttention 4 and PyTorch SDPA. But cross-attention called the FA4-only flash_attention() directly. Removing FA4 from the environment therefore avoided the import error while leaving an assertion waiting later in the run.

The relevant change is small:

- x = flash_attention(q, k, v, k_lens=context_lens)
+ x = attention(q, k, v, k_lens=context_lens)

Now cross-attention uses the same backend-selection boundary.

There is a semantic condition behind that edit. In the call path covered by the PR, context_lens is None, so the fallback computes full attention. The SDPA branch does not implement arbitrary variable-length padding masks. Routing a masked attention call through it would need additional work.

When FA4 is available, the dispatcher forwards the same arguments to the existing FA4 implementation.

The general lesson is to trace the callers. An optional backend is only optional if the execution paths that need it actually pass through the fallback.

3. Model loading had its own Unix dependency

The remaining fcntl dependency was outside attention.

The project stages base-model files and checkpoints into a local cache, using fcntl for file locking. The default staging path brought the same platform assumption back into the run.

The patch makes the import optional in both loading utilities. If fcntl is unavailable, staging is skipped and the model or checkpoint is loaded from its original path.

This preserves the underlying operation—reading the weights—without pretending that the Unix locking mechanism exists. It also avoids adding a new cross-platform lock implementation for a cache optimization.

On systems where fcntl exists, the existing staging path remains available. On systems where FA4 imports successfully, that attention path remains available too.

What the Windows run established

The PR records the following setup:

  • Windows 11 and RTX 5090.
  • Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128.
  • Other package versions from the project's uv.lock.
  • FCP 1.3B EMA checkpoint, sailboat example, seed 42, and a five-second duration request.

Before the patch, the run stopped at import. With the patch and SDPA, it produced 80 frames at 768×432, with 209 seconds of sampling, 231 seconds for the whole run, and 16.4 GiB peak allocated GPU memory.

One detail belongs beside those results: all reported runs used load_diffusion_pretrained=false. The PR explains that the EMA checkpoint strictly replaces every backbone weight, so the base DiT initialization does not determine the final output. This was not a claim that every model file or loading step could be omitted.

These numbers describe one tested example and environment. They are not an end-to-end validation of training, every checkpoint, or every GPU.

Preserving FA4 and comparing SDPA are different checks

The fallback needed to work, but the original fast path also needed a regression check.

For a controlled experiment, I made FA4 importable using triton-windows and a test-only no-op fcntl module. That shim is not in the PR and is not an installation recommendation—it does not provide real file locking.

With FA4 available, the original branch and the patched branch produced bit-identical decoded frames. That comparison checks whether the patch changed the existing FA4 path.

Comparing SDPA against FA4 answers a different question. On the same example, the first conditioning frame was identical, while frame PSNR was 33.5 dB on average and 31.6 dB at minimum. The generated results were not bit-identical.

FA4 sampling took 154 seconds, versus 209 seconds for SDPA. The fallback made the example runnable with a measurable speed tradeoff. It did not reproduce FA4's exact numerical output.

These are comparisons recorded in the PR's validation notes, not new experiments performed for this article.

The 5B follow-up found the next boundary

I also checked the 5B model with the paper-fan example and documented the result in a follow-up comment.

Sampling completed: 30 latent frames in 231 seconds, with 24.3 GiB peak allocated GPU memory.

The immediately following VAE decode did not fit in the same process on the tested 32 GB GPU / 64 GB RAM machine. The generator and both KV caches remained on the GPU; Windows commit charge passed 104 GiB, and I stopped the run.

Decoding those saved latents separately took 8.2 GiB and 11 seconds. That result points to a phase-lifetime and memory-management problem, beyond the portability fix in this PR.

So the precise outcome is: the 1.3B example completed end to end; the 5B example completed sampling, with decode checked in a separate process. The merge does not include a solution for the combined 5B memory peak.

What I would carry into the next portability fix

This patch connected three things: optional-backend detection, the callers that select that backend, and the platform-specific optimization in model loading.

For another research implementation, I would follow the same checks: attempt the optional import, trace every caller, verify that the fallback preserves the required attention semantics, log the selected path, and test the complete workload. A successful import is only the beginning.

The merged changes are small enough to read alongside the model's setup and inference instructions. FCP and the released models are the research authors' work; my contribution is getting this tested inference path through Windows without replacing the existing FA4 path.

Have you encountered an “optional” dependency that turned out to be mandatory through a different call site?
